name: Document incident declaration criteria and intake paths
description: Write down the severity and impact thresholds that turn a security event into an incident, name who may declare and stand down, and define intake for events reported outside monitoring.
responsible_role: CISO or equivalent, with Security Engineering drafting

steps.action: Define severity levels with concrete impact descriptions covering confidentiality, availability, and integrity.
State the threshold at which a security event is declared an incident.
Name who may declare an incident and who may stand one down, making both attributable.
Define intake paths for customer reports, researcher disclosures, vendor notifications, and staff reports.
Require the declaration basis to reference the criteria in every incident record.
Require non-incident dispositions to be recorded too, so the discriminating judgement is visible.

implementation_considerations: Criteria written too tightly produce declarations nobody makes; written too loosely they produce incidents for every alert. Calibrate against the last year of real events.
The stand-down decision is the one usually left undefined and is where inconsistency shows up first.
External intake paths need a monitored address and a named owner, not just a mention in the policy.
typical_duration: Days to draft; the calibration discussion is the substantive part.
prerequisites: An alert or event population to calibrate thresholds against

verification_method.how: Confirm documented criteria exist, and that incident records created after the change cite them as the declaration basis while non-incident dispositions are also recorded.

residual_risk_note: Documented criteria improve consistency; they do not guarantee the judgement is right in a novel situation.
period_limitation_note: Documenting criteria now does not make declarations during an elapsed period consistent or evidenced.
notes: No severity scheme is prescribed by SOC 2. The entity defines its own and is then measured against it.
